takeaways: Classify every column first: both slenderness ratios below 12 make it short; a ratio of 12 or more adds the additional moment about that axis.
Every column carries at least P<sub>u</sub>e<sub>min</sub>; the axial formula 0.4f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.67f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub> is only for e<sub>min</sub> ≤ 0.05D.
Ties follow three pitch limits: least lateral dimension, 16 times the smallest bar, 300 mm.
A load–moment point is safe inside the interaction curve; moment capacity peaks near the balanced load.
Biaxial bending uses capacities at the design P<sub>u</sub> and an exponent αn set by P<sub>u</sub>/P<sub>uz</sub>.
Footings are sized with service loads and designed with net factored pressure; their own weight causes no bending.
In footings one-way shear usually sets the depth; punching is checked at d/2 from the column.
A combined footing puts its centroid under the resultant, then needs top steel between the columns and transverse steel under each.
A retaining wall is checked as a rigid block (overturning, sliding, bearing) before its stem, heel and toe are designed.
Water tanks are designed for watertightness: low steel stress, small bars at close spacing, and enough concrete to limit tension.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for complete designs here: a short column with axial load and moments (with SP 16), and wall, isolated, sloped and combined footings. Marks go to the checks in the right order, the code limits by name and a neat reinforcement sketch.

bank.q: Classify reinforced concrete columns. Explain effective length, the short/slender limit, the minimum eccentricity and the additional moment of a slender column, with the IS 456 values.
outline: Classification by lateral steel, loading, shape and slenderness; pedestal
Effective length l<sub>e</sub> = Kl with the design K values
Short when l<sub>ex</sub>/D and l<sub>ey</sub>/b are both less than 12; limits 60b and 100b²/D
e<sub>min</sub> = l/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm and the 0.05D condition
Additional moment M<sub>a</sub> = P<sub>u</sub>D/2000 (l<sub>e</sub>/D)² and the factor k
A short numerical illustration
answer: A column is a vertical compression member whose effective length is more than three times its least lateral dimension (a shorter one is a pedestal). Classification comes first in every column design, because the class decides three things: whether the simple axial formula may be used, whether moments must be added, and whether a second-order (additional) moment is needed.

Classification. (a) By lateral reinforcement: tied columns (closed ties at a pitch), helically reinforced columns (continuous helix; 1.05 times the tied strength when the helix ratio is met) and composite columns (a steel section encased in concrete). (b) By loading: axially loaded, uniaxial bending, biaxial bending. (c) By shape: square, rectangular, circular, L or T. (d) By slenderness: short and slender. A pedestal is a compression member with effective length not more than three times its least lateral dimension.

answer.text: Effective length: the length that buckles, l<sub>e</sub> = K l, where l is the unsupported (clear) length. IS 456 Table 28 design values:

answer: Slenderness: a column is short when l<sub>ex</sub>/D < 12 and l<sub>ey</sub>/b < 12; otherwise it is slender about the axis that reaches 12. The unsupported length must not exceed 60 times the least lateral dimension, and for a column free at one end 100b²/D.

Minimum eccentricity (clause 25.4): every column is designed for e<sub>min</sub> = l/500 + D/30, not less than 20 mm, about each axis in turn. The simple axial formula P<sub>u</sub> = 0.4f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.67f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub> is allowed only when e<sub>min</sub> ≤ 0.05D.

Additional moment (clause 39.7): a slender column bows by about l<sub>e</sub>²/(2000D) under load, so M<sub>a</sub> = (P<sub>u</sub>D/2000)(l<sub>e</sub>/D)² is added to the first-order moment, about each slender axis. It may be multiplied by k = (P<sub>uz</sub> − P<sub>u</sub>)/(P<sub>uz</sub> − P<sub>b</sub>) ≤ 1, which is small for heavily loaded columns.

answer.text: Illustration: a 300 mm × 450 mm braced column, pinned at both ends, 3.6 m high.
answer.pre:
l<sub>ex</sub>/D = 3600/450 = 8.0 < 12   (short about x)
l<sub>ey</sub>/b = 3600/300 = 12.0, not < 12   (slender about y)
e<sub>min,x</sub> = 7.2 + 15.0 = 22.2 mm;  e<sub>min,y</sub> = 7.2 + 10.0 = 17.2 → 20 mm
at P<sub>u</sub> = 1200 kN: M<sub>ay</sub> = (1200 × 0.3/2000) × 12² = 25.92 kN·m

answer: How the class changes the design: a short column with only axial load (e<sub>min</sub> ≤ 0.05D) uses the axial formula; a short column with moments is designed from the interaction curve or SP 16; a slender column adds M<sub>a</sub> about each slender axis to its first-order moment and is then designed as a short column for the total. For a braced column the first-order moment taken with M<sub>a</sub> is 0.4M<sub>1</sub> + 0.6M<sub>2</sub> but not less than 0.4M<sub>2</sub>, where M<sub>2</sub> is the larger end moment (IS 456 clause 39.7.1).

Check: with 6 bars of 16 mm (M20, Fe415), P<sub>uz</sub> = 1580 kN and P<sub>b</sub> = 349 kN, so k = (1580 − 1200)/(1580 − 349) = 0.31 and the reduced additional moment is about 8.0 kN·m, a third of the unreduced value.

bank.q: Explain the interaction diagram of a rectangular column. For a 300 mm × 500 mm column with 8 bars of 20 mm on the two short faces (d′ = 58 mm, M20, Fe415), find the pure axial, balanced and pure bending points and sketch the curve.
outline: Axes P<sub>u</sub> and M<sub>u</sub>; safe region inside
Strain profiles: 0.0035 at the face; 0.002 at 3D/7 when x<sub>u</sub> > D
P<sub>uz</sub> = 0.45f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.75f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub>; design cap 0.4f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.67f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub>
Balanced point at steel strain 0.0038
Compression and tension failure zones
Pure bending as a doubly reinforced beam
Sketch with the computed points
answer: Assumptions (IS 456 clause 39.1): plane sections remain plane; the concrete strain is 0.0035 at the more compressed face while the neutral axis lies within the section, and 0.002 at 3D/7 from that face when the whole section is in compression; concrete has the parabola–rectangle design stress block with peak 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> and carries no tension; Fe415 bars follow the design stress–strain curve of SP 16. Each neutral-axis depth x<sub>u</sub> then gives one pair (P<sub>u</sub>, M<sub>u</sub>), with moments taken about the centroid of the section.
Data: A<sub>sc</sub> = 8 × 314.2 = 2513 mm² (1.68 %), half on each 300 mm face at d′ = 58 mm; A<sub>c</sub> = 147487 mm².

Pure axial load: P<sub>uz</sub> = 0.45 × 20 × 147487 + 0.75 × 415 × 2513 = 2109.6 kN. The code caps any column at the axial formula 0.4 × 20 × 147487 + 0.67 × 415 × 2513 = 1878.7 kN, which covers e<sub>min</sub>.

Neutral axis at the far face (x<sub>u</sub> = D = 500 mm): strain 0.0035 at the top and zero at the bottom face. Integrating the stress block and the bar forces gives P<sub>u</sub> = 1616 kN, M<sub>u</sub> = 110 kN·m.

Balanced point: tension steel strain 0.87 × 415/200 000 + 0.002 = 0.0038 with 0.0035 at the top, so x<sub>u,b</sub> = 0.0035/0.0073 × 442 = 211.9 mm. Concrete 0.36 × 20 × 300 × 211.9 = 457.7 kN; compression bars at strain 0.00254; tension bars at 360.9 N/mm². Result P<sub>b</sub> = 429 kN, M<sub>b</sub> = 243 kN·m.
Pure bending: the neutral axis that gives P<sub>u</sub> = 0 is at x<sub>u</sub> = 85 mm; the section acts as a doubly reinforced beam with M<sub>u0</sub> = 178 kN·m.

Shape: from pure bending the curve rises to the right (axial compression delays steel yielding: tension failure zone), reaches its widest point near the balanced load, then turns back towards the axial point (compression failure zone, where more load leaves less moment). A design point (P<sub>u</sub>, M<sub>u</sub>) inside the curve and below the cap is safe; the worked example in the chapter, (150 kN·m, 1200 kN), lies inside with the curve at about 174 kN·m at that load.

Using the curve: the designer reads the moment capacity at the design load and compares it with M<sub>u</sub>. SP 16 gives the same curves in non-dimensional form, P<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>bD) against M<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>bD²), one chart for each d′/D (0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20) with lines of p/f<sub>ck</sub>. For this column d′/D = 58/500 = 0.116 and p/f<sub>ck</sub> = 1.676/20 = 0.084, so it lies between the 0.10 and 0.15 charts.
Check: the balanced moment 243 kN·m is 1.36 times the pure bending moment 178 kN·m, the bulge expected of a symmetrically reinforced column, and P<sub>b</sub> = 429 kN is 20 % of P<sub>uz</sub>.

bank.q: Explain the critical sections for bending, one-way shear and punching shear in wall, isolated and combined footings, and why shear usually decides the depth. Illustrate with numbers.
outline: Bending at the face (concrete) or midway to the centre-line (masonry wall)
One-way shear at d from the face across the full width
Punching on a perimeter at d/2; k<sub>s</sub>0.25√f<sub>ck</sub>
Footings carry shear without stirrups; low τ<sub>c</sub>
Numbers from a 2.7 m × 2.5 m pad
Combined footing: shear at d from the faces in the beam direction
answer: Why critical sections matter: a footing is an inverted slab loaded upward by the soil and held down by the column or wall. It has no stirrups, so the concrete alone carries shear, and the checks below are what fix its depth; bending then fixes the steel.
Loads: all three checks use the net factored soil pressure w<sub>u</sub> = P<sub>u</sub>/A (the footing weight is excluded because it causes no bending).

Bending (IS 456 clause 34.2.3.2): the critical section is the face of a concrete column, pedestal or wall; for a masonry wall it is halfway between the centre-line and the face. The moment is taken on the full width of the footing.

One-way shear (clause 34.2.4.1(a)): a vertical section at distance d from the face, across the full width; τ<sub>v</sub> = V<sub>u</sub>/(Bd) ≤ τ<sub>c</sub> from Table 19 with the steel provided at that section.

Punching (two-way) shear (clause 34.2.4.1(b) with 31.6): a perimeter d/2 from the faces of the column; V<sub>u</sub> = P<sub>u</sub> − w<sub>u</sub>(a + d)(b + d); τ<sub>v</sub> = V<sub>u</sub>/(2(a + b + 2d)d) ≤ k<sub>s</sub> 0.25√f<sub>ck</sub>, k<sub>s</sub> = 0.5 + b/a ≤ 1. It does not arise for a continuous wall.

answer.text: Numbers (rectangular pad of the chapter: 300 × 500 column, 2.7 m × 2.5 m, w<sub>u</sub> = 266.67 kN/m², M20):

answer: Why shear governs: footing steel ratios are small (0.15 to 0.25 %), so τ<sub>c</sub> is only about 0.28 to 0.36 N/mm² for M20, while the slab must carry the whole column load out to the edges. Stirrups are impractical in a slab, so the depth is increased instead (or the grade raised).

Combined footing: the long direction is a beam; one-way shear at d from each column face usually governs, and the steel that counts for τ<sub>c</sub> is the steel in tension at that section (top bars where the moment hogs). Punching is checked under the heavier column.

Bending
One-way shear
Punching
rows: d from the face, each way
under columns and at V = 0 (beam); column faces (transverse)

answer: Order of working: size from service load, find w<sub>u</sub>, choose D from one-way shear, check punching, then find the steel at the face and check the development length beyond it. Raising D lowers both shear stresses; adding steel helps one-way shear a little (τ<sub>c</sub> grows with p<sub>t</sub>) but does nothing for punching.
Check: in the pad above, raising D from 550 to 600 mm moved τ<sub>v</sub> from 0.339 to 0.283 N/mm² while τ<sub>c</sub> stayed near 0.29 to 0.32 N/mm², which is why 600 mm was adopted.

bank.q: Design a braced short square tied column, 3.0 m unsupported length, for a factored axial load of 1500 kN using M25 concrete and Fe415 steel. Give the section, the bars and the ties, with a sketch.
outline: Trial area from 1 % steel
Check e<sub>min</sub> ≤ 0.05D before using the axial formula
Steel from the formula, raised to 0.8 % minimum
Bars, capacity check
Ties: diameter and the three pitch limits
Sketch
answer: Data: P<sub>u</sub> = 1500 kN, unsupported length 3.0 m, braced, f<sub>ck</sub> = 25 N/mm², f<sub>y</sub> = 415 N/mm². Assumed: no applied moment, so the column is designed for axial load if e<sub>min</sub> ≤ 0.05D; clear cover 40 mm to the main bars (IS 456 clause 26.4.2.1); l<sub>e</sub> = l for a braced column with both ends held in position.
Trial area: with p = 1 %, P<sub>u</sub> = A<sub>g</sub>(0.4 × 25 × 0.99 + 0.67 × 415 × 0.01) = A<sub>g</sub> × 12.68, so A<sub>g</sub> = 1 500 000/12.68 = 118292 mm², a side of 344 mm.

Section: a 350 mm side gives e<sub>min</sub> = 3000/500 + 350/30 = 17.7 → 20 mm > 0.05 × 350 = 17.5 mm, so the axial formula would not apply. Adopt 400 mm × 400 mm: e<sub>min</sub> = 6.0 + 13.3 = 19.3 → 20 mm = 0.05 × 400. Slenderness 3000/400 = 7.5 < 12 (short).
Steel: A<sub>sc</sub> = (1 500 000 − 0.4 × 25 × 160 000)/(278.05 − 10) = -373 mm², negative, so concrete alone is enough and the minimum governs: 0.008 × 160 000 = 1280 mm².
Bars: 4 bars of 20 mm give 1257 mm², just short. Provide 8 bars of 16 mm (3 per face): 1608 mm², 1.01 %.

Ties: diameter ≥ max(16/4 = 4 mm, 6 mm) → use 8 mm. Pitch ≤ least of 400 mm (side), 16 × 16 = 256 mm, 300 mm → 256 mm; adopt 250 mm. Here 16φ governs. The middle bar of each face is (400 − 2 × 56)/2 = 144 mm from the corners, more than 75 mm, so a diamond or single link ties the four middle bars.

bank.q: A 230 mm brick wall carries a factored load of 200 kN per metre run. Design a wall footing for a safe bearing capacity of 200 kN/m², using M20 concrete and Fe415 steel.
outline: Service load = factored/1.5; width with 10 % self-weight
Net factored pressure
Critical section halfway between wall centre and face (masonry)
Depth from bending and one-way shear at d from the face
Main steel, minimum steel; development length decides the bar size
Distribution steel and sketch
answer: Data: factored load 200 kN per metre run from a 230 mm brick wall, safe bearing capacity 200 kN/m², M20 and Fe415. Work on a 1 m length of wall. Assumed: self-weight of footing and backfill 10 % of the service load for sizing only; clear cover 50 mm to the bottom bars; τ<sub>bd</sub> = 1.2 × 1.6 N/mm² for deformed bars in M20.
Net factored pressure: w<sub>u</sub> = 200/0.8 = 250.0 kN/m². Projection beyond the wall face (B − t)/2 = 0.285 m.
Critical section for moment (masonry wall): 0.285 + 0.23/4 = 0.3425 m from the edge; M<sub>u</sub> = 250.0 × 0.3425²/2 = 14.66 kN·m/m.
Depth: d ≥ √(14.66 × 10⁶/(0.138 × 20 × 1000)) = 72.9 mm. Try D = 200 mm. The short projection limits the bar size (see the anchorage step), so use 8 mm bars: d = 200 − 50 − 4 = 146 mm.
Steel: A<sub>st</sub> = 290 mm²/m; minimum 0.12 % = 240 mm²/m. Provide 8 mm at 170 mm c/c = 296 mm²/m (p<sub>t</sub> = 0.203 %).

One-way shear at d from the wall face: x = 0.285 − 0.146 = 0.139 m; V<sub>u</sub> = 250.0 × 0.139 = 34.8 kN/m; τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.238 N/mm²; τ<sub>c</sub> (M20, p<sub>t</sub> 0.20 %) = 0.322 N/mm². Safe.

Anchorage: available beyond the critical section 342.5 − 50 = 292.5 mm. A 10 mm bar needs L<sub>d</sub> = 47 × 10 = 470 mm, far too long. An 8 mm bar needs 376 mm; a standard U hook at each end adds an anchorage value of 16φ = 128 mm (IS 456 clause 26.2.2.1), giving 292.5 + 128 = 420.5 mm ≥ 376 mm. So 8 mm bars with end hooks.
Distribution steel along the wall: 0.0012 × 1000 × 200 = 240 mm²/m → 8 mm at 200 mm c/c (251 mm²/m). Edge thickness 200 mm ≥ 150 mm.
Soil check with the real weight: (133.3 + 0.2 × 0.8 × 25)/0.8 = 171.7 kN/m² ≤ 200.

answer: Why the masonry rule: a brick wall cannot bend with the footing and may crush at its edges, so the bearing spreads a little into the wall. IS 456 clause 34.2.3.2 therefore moves the critical section halfway from the face towards the centre-line, a quarter of the wall thickness inside the face, which gives a slightly larger moment than at the face.

bank.q: Design a square isolated footing for a 400 mm × 400 mm column carrying a factored load of 1200 kN. Safe bearing capacity 180 kN/m², M25 concrete and Fe415 steel. Check one-way and punching shear.
outline: Service load and plan size with self-weight
Net factored pressure
Moment at the column face
Depth from one-way and punching shear
Steel each way, minimum steel, L<sub>d</sub>
Bearing under the column, sketch
answer: Data: 400 mm square column, P<sub>u</sub> = 1200 kN (service 800 kN), safe bearing capacity 180 kN/m², M25 and Fe415. Assumed: clear cover 50 mm; 10 % of the service load for self-weight in sizing; design pressure is the net factored pressure on the plan area actually adopted.
Moment at the face: 237.0 × 0.925²/2 = 101.41 kN·m/m, i.e. 228.2 kN·m on the full width. Depth for bending √(101.41 × 10⁶/(0.138 × 25 × 1000)) = 171 mm.
Shear decides. With D = 450 mm one-way shear gives τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.328 > τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.321 N/mm². Adopt D = 475 mm, d = 475 − 50 − 12 = 413 mm (12 mm bars, average of the layers).
One-way shear at d from the face: V<sub>u</sub> = 237.0 × 2.25 × (0.925 − 0.413) = 273.1 kN; τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.294 ≤ τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.304 N/mm² (with the steel below).
Steel each way: A<sub>st</sub> = 1574 mm² (minimum 0.12 % = 1282 mm²) → 14 bars of 12 mm = 1583 mm², spacing about 165 mm, both ways (square footing: uniform).
Development length: 12 mm bar, L<sub>d</sub> = 0.87 × 415 × 12/(4 × 1.4 × 1.6) = 484 mm (τ<sub>bd</sub> = 1.4 × 1.6 for M25) < 925 − 50 = 875 mm available.
Bearing under the column: 1200 × 10³/(400 × 400) = 7.5 N/mm² ≤ 0.45 × 25 × 2 = 22.5 N/mm² (√(A<sub>1</sub>/A<sub>2</sub>) capped at 2). Column bars need no extra dowels for bearing.

bank.q: Design a sloped square footing for a 400 mm square column carrying a service load of 1000 kN on soil of safe bearing capacity 200 kN/m². Use M20 concrete and Fe415 steel, and compare its concrete volume with a flat footing.
outline: Plan size from service load
Net factored pressure and moment at the face
Depth at the face with the compression width limited to the flat top
Edge thickness ≥ 150 mm; slope geometry
One-way shear at d on the sloped section; punching at d/2 with the depth there
Steel, anchorage, concrete saved
answer: Plan: A = 1.1 × 1000/200 = 5.50 m², side √5.5 = 2.35 m; adopt 2.4 m × 2.4 m. Net factored pressure w<sub>u</sub> = 1500/5.76 = 260.4 kN/m². Projection from the column face 1.0 m.
Moment at the column face on the full width: M<sub>u</sub> = 260.4 × 2.4 × 1.0²/2 = 312.5 kN·m.

Geometry: a flat top 550 mm square (75 mm ledge round the column for formwork), then a slope down to the edge. Only the concrete above the neutral axis resists compression, and at the face the top is only 550 mm wide, so take b = 550 mm for the depth check: d ≥ √(312.5 × 10⁶/(0.138 × 20 × 550)) = 454 mm.
Shear on the slope needs more. Adopt D = 700 mm at the column and 200 mm at the edge (above the 150 mm minimum); d = 700 − 50 − 12 = 638 mm at the face.

Steel: A<sub>st</sub> = 1487 mm² (with b = 550 mm), minimum 0.12 % of the trapezoidal section at the face (1218 × 10³ mm²) = 1461 mm². Provide 14 bars of 12 mm = 1583 mm² each way, spread over the full 2.4 m (the bars are in tension at the bottom, where the section is full width).

One-way shear at d from the face, 0.838 m from the centre: V<sub>u</sub> = 260.4 × 2.4 × (1.2 − 0.838) = 226.2 kN. The footing there is 396 mm deep at mid-width and thinner towards the corners; summing width × effective depth across the section gives 730 × 10³ mm². τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.310 N/mm²; τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.334 N/mm² for p<sub>t</sub> = 0.217 %. Safe.
Punching at d/2 = 319 mm from the face: the depth there is 568 mm, d = 506 mm. V<sub>u</sub> = 1500 − 260.4 × 1.038² = 1219.4 kN; b<sub>0</sub> = 4152 mm; τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.580 ≤ 1.118 N/mm².

Bending check: M<sub>u,lim</sub> on the flat top = 0.138 × 20 × 550 × 638² = 617.9 kN·m ≥ 312.5 kN·m, so the narrow compression zone is enough. Anchorage: L<sub>d</sub> of 12 mm = 47 × 12 = 564 mm < 1000 − 50 = 950 mm.
Concrete: the sloped footing holds 2.38 m³; a flat 2.4 m × 2.4 m × 700 mm slab would hold 4.03 m³. Saving 41 %.

bank.q: Two 400 mm square columns, 4.0 m apart, carry factored loads of 800 kN and 1200 kN. The safe bearing capacity is 200 kN/m². Design a rectangular combined footing with uniform pressure (projection beyond the lighter column 0.6 m), in M20 concrete and Fe415 steel.

Resultant and length for uniform pressure
Factored line load; SFD and BMD values
Depth from shear and punching; shear steel where τ<sub>v</sub> > τ<sub>c</sub>
Top, bottom and transverse steel
Sketch of the reinforcement
answer: Factored pressure q<sub>u</sub> = 2000/(6.0 × 1.25) = 266.7 kN/m²; w = 266.7 × 1.25 = 333.3 kN/m.

answer.text: Shear and moment (x from the end beyond the 800 kN column):

answer: Depth: try D = 800 mm, d = 742 mm. Punching at the 1200 kN column: V<sub>u</sub> = 1200 − 266.7 × 1.142² = 852.2 kN, τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.251 ≤ 1.118 N/mm².

Longitudinal steel: bottom under column 2 for 327 kN·m: A<sub>st</sub> = 1255 mm² (minimum 1200) → 7 bars of 16 mm. Top for 480 kN·m: A<sub>st</sub> = 1870 mm² → 12 bars of 16 mm = 2413 mm² (p<sub>t</sub> = 0.260 %).

One-way shear: at d from the left face of column 2 (x = 3.66 m) V<sub>u</sub> = 419.3 kN in a hogging zone, τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.452 N/mm² > τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.365 N/mm². The footing is only 1.25 m wide, so it is a true beam: provide stirrups for V<sub>us</sub> = 419.3 − 0.365 × 1250 × 742/1000 = 80.9 kN.

Stirrups: 4-legged 10 mm, A<sub>sv</sub> = 314 mm². Strength: s ≤ 0.87 × 415 × 314 × 742/80922 = 1040 mm; minimum shear steel: s ≤ 0.87 × 415 × 314/(0.4 × 1250) = 227 mm; and ≤ 0.75d, 300 mm. Provide 4-legged 10 mm stirrups at 220 mm c/c over the region where τ<sub>v</sub> > τ<sub>c</sub> (between the columns near column 2), and the minimum stirrups elsewhere. Near column 1, τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.308 N/mm² < 0.365 N/mm², so minimum stirrups only.

Transverse: cantilever (1.25 − 0.4)/2 = 0.425 m; under column 2, M<sub>u</sub> = (1200/1.25) × 0.425²/2 = 86.7 kN·m over a strip 0.4 + 2 × 0.742 = 1.884 m wide needs only 332 mm², so the minimum 0.12 % of 1000 × 800 = 960 mm²/m governs: 12 mm bars at 110 mm c/c (1028 mm²/m) on top of the bottom longitudinal bars, full length.

answer: Check: total upward force 333.3 × 6.0 = 2000 kN = 800 + 1200; moment of the soil load about column 1, 2000 × (3.0 − 0.6) = 4800 kN·m, equals 1200 × 4 = 4800 kN·m, so the pressure is uniform.

bank.q: A braced short column 350 mm × 500 mm, 3.2 m long, carries P<sub>u</sub> = 1100 kN, M<sub>ux</sub> = 110 kN·m (about the major axis) and M<sub>uy</sub> = 60 kN·m. Design it with M25 and Fe415, bars spread on four faces.
outline: Minimum eccentricity moments about each axis
Trial steel at about 1 %
M<sub>ux1</sub> and M<sub>uy1</sub> at P<sub>u</sub> (chart or strain compatibility)
P<sub>uz</sub> and αn
Load-contour check
Ties and sketch
answer: Method (IS 456 clause 39.6): a column under axial load with moments about both axes is checked on the load contour at the design load. Find the uniaxial capacities M<sub>ux1</sub> and M<sub>uy1</sub> at P<sub>u</sub> with the trial steel, find P<sub>uz</sub> and the exponent αn, and require (M<sub>ux</sub>/M<sub>ux1</sub>)<sup>αn</sup> + (M<sub>uy</sub>/M<sub>uy1</sub>)<sup>αn</sup> ≤ 1. Each applied moment must be at least P<sub>u</sub>e<sub>min</sub> about its own axis.

Minimum eccentricities: e<sub>x</sub> = 3200/500 + 500/30 = 23.1 mm, e<sub>y</sub> = 6.4 + 350/30 = 18.1 → 20 mm. Minimum moments 1100 × 0.0231 = 25.4 and 1100 × 0.020 = 22.0 kN·m, both below the applied moments.
Trial: 8 bars of 16 mm (4 corners and the middle of each face): A<sub>sc</sub> = 1608 mm², p = 0.92 % (above 0.8 %). d′ = 40 + 8 + 8 = 56 mm.
Non-dimensional load: P<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>bD) = 1 100 000/(25 × 350 × 500) = 0.251, near the balanced region, where the moment capacity is largest.

Uniaxial capacities at 1100 kN (strain compatibility, three layers of bars: 3, 2 and 3): M<sub>ux1</sub> = 190.8 kN·m (depth 500 mm) and M<sub>uy1</sub> = 124.3 kN·m (depth 350 mm). Each applied moment is below its capacity.
Ties: 8 mm (≥ 16/4 and ≥ 6 mm); pitch ≤ least of 350 mm, 16 × 16 = 256 mm and 300 mm, so 250 mm. The middle bars sit more than 75 mm from the corners, so each has a link.

Why the exponent matters: with αn = 1 the contour would be a straight line and the check would read 110/190.8 + 60/124.3 = 1.059. With αn = 1.41 the contour bulges outward, nearer a quarter circle, and the same moments give 0.816. The higher the load ratio P<sub>u</sub>/P<sub>uz</sub>, the more the contour bulges.

head: Item
Value
rows: 8 mm at 250 mm c/c with links

answer: Check: with fewer bars the steel would fall below 0.8 % (1400 mm²), so 8 bars of 16 mm is also near the economical minimum. The margin 0.18 in the contour sum covers chart-reading error.

bank.q: A braced short circular column of 450 mm diameter, 3.5 m long, carries P<sub>u</sub> = 1000 kN with M<sub>ux</sub> = 60 kN·m and M<sub>uy</sub> = 80 kN·m. Design the longitudinal bars and lateral ties using M25 and Fe415.
outline: Resultant moment for a circular section
Minimum eccentricity moment
Minimum steel 0.8 % and at least 6 bars
Moment capacity at P<sub>u</sub> in the weaker bar orientation
Circular ties: diameter and pitch
answer: Data: D = 450 mm, l = 3.5 m, braced, P<sub>u</sub> = 1000 kN, M<sub>ux</sub> = 60 kN·m, M<sub>uy</sub> = 80 kN·m, M25 and Fe415. Assumed: clear cover 40 mm, 8 mm ties, so the bar centres are 40 + 8 + 8 = 56 mm from the surface.
A circular section with equally spaced bars has the same capacity about every diameter, so combine the moments: M<sub>u</sub> = √(60² + 80²) = 100 kN·m.
Minimum eccentricity: 3500/500 + 450/30 = 22.0 mm, so P<sub>u</sub>e<sub>min</sub> = 22 kN·m < 100 kN·m. Slenderness 3500/450 = 7.8 < 12: short.
A<sub>g</sub> = π × 450²/4 = 159043 mm²; minimum steel 0.8 % = 1272 mm². 6 bars of 16 mm give 1206 mm² (0.76 %), below the minimum.
Use 8 bars of 16 mm: 1608 mm² (1.01 %), d′ = 56 mm, bars on a circle of radius 169 mm.

Capacity at 1000 kN by strain compatibility (integrating the stress block over the circular segment and adding each bar): 126.6 kN·m with a bar on the bending axis and 127.7 kN·m with the bars turned by half a spacing. Take the smaller, 126.6 kN·m ≥ 100 kN·m.
Ties: circular ties of 8 mm (≥ 16/4 = 4 mm and ≥ 6 mm). Pitch ≤ least of 450 mm, 16 × 16 = 256 mm and 300 mm, so 250 mm. A helix is not needed: the factor 1.05 helps only axial strength.

Why the weaker orientation: the capacity of a circle with few bars depends slightly on how the bars sit relative to the bending axis. Here the two orientations differ by 1.0 kN·m. The column cannot know which way the resultant moment acts, so the smaller value is used.
Helix or ties: a helix meeting clause 39.4 would raise only the axial strength by 5 %; under a moment this size the column is governed by bending, so circular ties are the economical choice.

Check: the capacity ratio 100/126.6 = 0.79; P<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>D²) = 1 000 000/(25 × 450²) = 0.198 and M<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>D³) = 0.0439, the numbers used to enter an SP 16 circular-column chart.

bank.q: A braced column 300 mm × 400 mm has effective length 4.2 m about both axes. It carries P<sub>u</sub> = 900 kN and a first-order moment of 30 kN·m about the minor axis. Show whether it is slender, find the design moment and design the steel (M25, Fe415, bars on the two 400 mm faces).
outline: Slenderness ratios about both axes
Additional moment about the slender axis
P<sub>uz</sub>, P<sub>b</sub> and the factor k
Total design moment versus P<sub>u</sub>e<sub>min</sub>
Capacity from strain compatibility or SP 16
Ties; comment on the effect of slenderness
answer: Method: classify about each axis; about a slender axis add M<sub>a</sub> (IS 456 clause 39.7.1), reduced by k when P<sub>u</sub> exceeds the balanced load; then design the section as a short column for the total moment. Cover 40 mm and 8 mm ties are assumed.
Ratios: l<sub>ex</sub>/D = 4200/400 = 10.5 < 12 (short about x); l<sub>ey</sub>/b = 4200/300 = 14.0 ≥ 12, so the column is slender about the minor axis only.
Additional moment about y: M<sub>ay</sub> = (P<sub>u</sub>b/2000)(l<sub>ey</sub>/b)² = (900 × 0.3/2000) × 14² = 0.135 × 196 = 26.46 kN·m.
Trial steel: 0.8 % of 120 000 = 960 mm²; 4 bars of 16 mm (804 mm²) are too few, so use 4 bars of 20 mm, 1257 mm² (1.05 %), two on each 400 mm face, d′ = 58 mm.
P<sub>b</sub> about y: x<sub>u,b</sub> = 0.0035/0.0073 × (300 − 58) = 116.0 mm; concrete, compression bars and yielded tension bars give P<sub>b</sub> = 382.7 kN.

Design moment about y: 30 + 16.28 = 46.28 kN·m (more than P<sub>u</sub>e<sub>min</sub> = 900 × 0.020 = 18 kN·m). About x only e<sub>min</sub> applies (4200/500 + 400/30 = 21.7 mm, 19.5 kN·m), checked separately.

Capacity about y at 900 kN with 4 bars of 20 mm: strain compatibility gives M<sub>uy1</sub> = 73.1 kN·m ≥ 46.28 kN·m. Safe. (SP 16 entry values: P<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>bD) = 0.30, M<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>Db²) = 0.051, d′/b = 0.19.)
Ties: 8 mm (≥ 20/4 = 5 and 6 mm); pitch ≤ least of 300 mm, 16 × 20 = 320 mm and 300 mm, so 300 mm.

Comment: slenderness raised the design moment from 30 to 46.3 kN·m, by 54 %. Without the factor k the moment would be 56.5 kN·m. Check: k is below 1 because P<sub>u</sub> = 900 kN is well above P<sub>b</sub> = 383 kN.

bank.q: A cantilever wall retains 4.0 m of level dry sand (γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30°), measured to the underside of the base. Base 2.4 m wide and 0.3 m thick with a 0.8 m toe; stem 0.25 m thick. μ = 0.55, q<sub>s</sub> = 150 kN/m². Evaluate overturning, sliding and bearing, and state why these come before the design of the stem and base.
outline: Active thrust ½K<sub>a</sub>γH² at H/3
Weights and moments about the toe in a table
Overturning and sliding with the 0.9/1.4 rule of IS 456 clause 20
Eccentricity and base pressures
Remedy for any check that fails
Why stability comes first
answer: Data and assumptions: Rankine earth pressure on a vertical plane through the heel, wall friction ignored, level dry backfill, analysis per metre length of wall; concrete 25 kN/m³; passive soil in front of the toe ignored except at the shear key. IS 456 clause 20 requires 0.9 × restoring ≥ 1.4 × overturning, for moments and for sliding forces.
Earth pressure: K<sub>a</sub> = (1 − sin 30°)/(1 + sin 30°) = 1/3. P<sub>a</sub> = ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 4.0² = 48.0 kN/m at 4.0/3 = 1.333 m; M<sub>O</sub> = 64.0 kN·m/m.

answer.text: Stabilising weights (stem height 3.7 m, heel 1.35 m):

answer: Overturning: 0.9 × 198.1 = 178.3 ≥ 1.4 × 64.0 = 89.6 kN·m. Safe; plain factor of safety 3.10.
Sliding: 0.9 × 0.55 × 131.0 = 64.9 kN < 1.4 × 48.0 = 67.2 kN. Fails narrowly (plain factor 1.50, which would pass a 1.5 rule but not clause 20). Short by 2.6 kN of friction.

Remedy: a shear key 0.3 m deep under the stem. Passive resistance in front of it (K<sub>p</sub> = 3, from 0.3 m to 0.6 m below the toe level, soil above the toe ignored) is ½ × 3 × 18 × (0.6² − 0.3²) = 7.29 kN/m, more than the 2.6 kN needed.
Stem (for completeness): M<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × (1/3) × 18 × 3.7³/6 = 76.0 kN·m/m; with d = 194 mm, A<sub>st</sub> = 1253 mm²/m on the soil face.

Why first: the stem, heel and toe moments depend on the base width, the toe length and the pressures under the base. If the wall overturns, slides or overloads the soil, the base must be resized, and every member moment changes. So the rigid-body checks fix the geometry; member design follows.

Reading the result: friction alone gives a plain factor of 1.50, but IS 456 asks for 0.9 × resistance ≥ 1.4 × force, which is the same as a plain factor of 1.4/0.9 = 1.56. The wall is therefore short of resistance even though it would pass the older factor of 1.5. Other remedies are a wider heel (more soil weight on the base) or a rougher, deeper founding level; the key is cheapest because it adds passive resistance without changing the stem or the bearing pressures much.
Verdict: overturning and bearing pass with margin; sliding needs the key. Check: ΣW × x = 131.0 × 1.023 = 134.1 = M<sub>R</sub> − M<sub>O</sub> = 134.1 kN·m.

bank.q: A circular water tank of 10 m internal diameter holds water 4 m deep and rests on a flexible base joint. Design the wall (M30, Fe415), giving the hoop steel at 1 m intervals, and explain why the steel stress is kept low.
outline: Pressure and hoop tension T = γ<sub>w</sub>hr at each level
Steel at 130 N/mm² (IS 3370 Part 2)
Thickness for no cracking with σ<sub>ct</sub> = 1.5 N/mm² and practical minimum
Minimum steel and spacing rules
Vertical steel
Why low steel stress
answer: Data: internal diameter 10 m (r = 5 m), water depth 4 m, flexible base joint, M30 and Fe415. Working-stress values from IS 3370 (Part 2): σ<sub>st</sub> = 130 N/mm² for deformed bars; σ<sub>ct</sub> = 1.5 N/mm² in direct tension; σ<sub>cbc</sub> = 10 N/mm², so m = 280/(3 × 10) = 9.33 and m − 1 = 8.33. γ<sub>w</sub> = 10 kN/m³.
Hoop tension at depth h: T = 10 × h × 5 = 50h kN/m. At the base T = 200 kN/m.
Thickness: no-crack check 200000/(1000t + 8.33 × 1538) ≤ 1.5 gives t ≥ 121 mm. The rule 30H + 50 = 170 mm and two layers of bars with 45 mm cover lead to t = 200 mm.

answer.text: Hoop steel (A<sub>s</sub> = T/130, two layers because t ≥ 200 mm, spacing ≤ 200 mm = t):

answer: Minimum steel: tank under 15 m, so 0.24 % of 1000 × 200 = 480 mm²/m in each direction; the top metre is governed by it.
Concrete tension at the base: 200000/(1000 × 200 + 8.33 × 1616) = 0.94 N/mm² ≤ 1.5. Safe.

Vertical steel: the flexible base means no vertical bending, so the minimum 480 mm²/m: 8 mm bars at 200 mm c/c on each face (503 mm²/m). Base slab on the ground: minimum steel both ways, with a water bar at the wall joint.

Why low stress: steel strain at working load sets the crack width. At 130 N/mm² the strain is 130/200 000 = 0.00065, and with small bars at close spacing the cracks stay within 0.2 mm, the limit IS 3370 sets for liquid-retaining faces. At a limit-state stress of 0.87 × 415 = 361 N/mm² the cracks would be nearly three times wider and the tank would leak.

Detailing: hoop bars lapped in a staggered pattern so that no two adjacent bars are lapped at the same section; clear cover 45 mm on both faces; vertical bars outside the hoops on the outer face only where convenient. Cast the wall in lifts with a water bar at every horizontal joint, and test by filling before any finish is applied.

glossary.def: A column in a frame held against sideways movement by walls, bracing or a core, so its effective length is at most its clear length.
A column whose ends can move sideways; its effective length is more than its clear length.
A compression member whose effective length is not more than three times its least lateral dimension.
The clear height of a column between the floor and the underside of the beam or slab that holds it sideways.
A closed loop of small bar round the longitudinal bars that stops them buckling and holds them in place.
A continuous spiral of bar round the core of a circular column that confines the concrete.
The diameter of a helically reinforced column measured to the outside of the helix.
The load at which concrete reaches 0.0035 strain as the tension steel reaches its limiting strain; the interaction curve is widest near it.
The curve of axial load against moment capacity for one section and steel arrangement.
The Bureau of Indian Standards handbook of design aids for reinforced concrete, with charts and tables for beams, slabs and columns.
The curve of M<sub>ux</sub> against M<sub>uy</sub> at a fixed axial load, approximated by the exponent αn.
The pressure the soil can carry with an adequate margin against shear failure and excess settlement.
The upward soil pressure from the factored column load only, used for footing design.
The section where a check is made: the face for bending, d from the face for one-way shear, d/2 for punching.
A footing whose top slopes from the column to a thinner edge to save concrete.
One footing carrying two or more columns.
Two pads joined by a stiff beam so that an eccentric pad at a boundary is balanced by an inner one.
A downstand under a retaining wall base that adds passive resistance against sliding.
The parts of a retaining wall base behind and in front of the stem.
The ring tension in a circular tank wall caused by water pressure.
A strip of rubber or PVC cast across a construction joint to stop water seeping through.
m = 280/(3σ<sub>cbc</sub>), used to add the steel to the concrete area in working-stress checks.
